title: Building This Blog: A Case Study in Contract-Driven Development
excerpt: How an AI coding agent and a human turned 8 disconnected prompts into a coherent system by adding a missing phase — the design system — and rewriting everything around explicit contracts.
content:
I'm building this blog in the open. Not the polished "look how easy it was" version — the real one, with false starts, abandoned plans, and a major rework three phases in. This post documents what happened so far.

The starting point

The project began with a Spec-Driven Development approach: a SPEC.md describing the product, an ARCHITECTURE.md defining the tech stack, and eight implementation prompts — one per phase. The stack is Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Prisma 7 on Neon PostgreSQL, Tailwind 4, and Auth.js v5.

The prompts were thorough. Each one walked through exact file paths, code snippets, and verification steps. On the surface, they looked like a complete blueprint.

Phase 1 and 2: smooth sailing

Phase 1 built the data layer — a Prisma schema with ten models (User, Post, Tag, Comment, Bookmark, Translation, and their join tables), a Prisma client singleton wired to Neon via the serverless adapter, and a small set of API response helpers.

Phase 2 added authentication. Auth.js v5 with GitHub and Google OAuth, a Prisma adapter, JWT sessions, a custom sign-in page. This is where the first cracks showed: the original prompt installed next-auth@beta (v5) but wrote v4 API code. The NextAuthOptions type, the getServerSession(authOptions) pattern, the route handler export — all v4. We adapted to the real v5 API: NextAuth() returning { handlers, signIn, signOut, auth }, the auth() function replacing getServerSession.

Auth worked. We committed and moved on.

The disease

Then came the question that changed the trajectory: "is this sign-in page okay?"

The sign-in page was functionally correct but architecturally symptomatic. Every button was an inline-styled <div>. Every card was a hand-rolled container with style={{ backgroundColor: 'var(--bg-raised)', border: '1px solid var(--border)' }}. The same patterns repeated in the Header, and were about to repeat again in comments, bookmarks, and the about page.

By Phase 8, we'd have had fifteen components with duplicated styling and no way to change a button radius without editing eight files.

The architecture docs promised shadcn/ui. The prompts forbade it. Nothing bridged the two. Each prompt optimized for "make this one phase work in isolation" rather than "build a coherent system."

The cure: Phase 0 and contracts

We stopped and inserted a new foundation phase. Phase 0 installs shadcn/ui primitives — Button, Card, Badge, Input, Avatar, Skeleton — and maps them to the project's existing design tokens via an alias layer. Our tokens (--bg-base, --ink-primary) remain the source of truth. shadcn's tokens (--background, --foreground) reference them. Both naming systems coexist.

Then we rewrote all eight prompts with a contract-driven structure. Every phase now declares four sections at the top:

  • Consumes — what it needs from earlier phases (exact imports)
  • Produces — what it creates (files, exports, routes)
  • Does NOT Build — explicit anti-scope to prevent reinvention
  • Contracts — component prop signatures, function signatures, type definitions

The result: Phase 7 (Home & About) can consume Phase 4's <PostCard> without reading its source. The PostSummary type flows directly from getPublishedPosts() into <PostCard post={post} />. No guessing, no drift.

Phase 3: routing and i18n

Phase 3 added next-intl with locale prefixes (/en/, /fa/). Every route moved under [locale]/. The Header got a language switcher. Translations live in messages/en.json and messages/fa.json.

The tricky part: Auth.js's pages.signIn config can't take a dynamic locale path. We removed it and let the Header's sign-in button use next-intl's typed Link component, which auto-prepends the locale. A trade-off for Phase 6 to handle when protected routes appear.

Phase 4: where contracts paid off

The blog feature is where the contract approach proved itself. The PostSummary type includes readingTime as a pre-computed string — computed in the service layer, not the component. The original prompt had a bug here: it excluded content from PostSummary, then tried to compute reading time from it in the component. The contract caught this before any code was written.

The Prisma schema uses explicit join tables (PostTag, not implicit many-to-many), so the service layer handles the mapping: include: { tags: { include: { tag: true } } } then flatten to Tag[]. Components never see the join table.

What's next

Three static posts were migrated from .tsx files into the database via a seed script. This very post was created through the POST /api/posts endpoint — a live test of the route handler, the service layer, and the Prisma adapter.

Phases 5 through 8 remain: comments (threaded, anonymous + authenticated), bookmarks, the home and about pages, and polish (error boundaries, loading skeletons, ESLint). Each one will consume the primitives and contracts established in Phase 0.

The lesson: a series of self-contained prompts produces a series of self-contained silos. Explicit contracts — declared upfront, verified at every phase boundary — are what turn isolated steps into a coherent system.
